rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: He described passing a caravan near al-Rawḥāʾ whose people had lost a camel, and drinking from their water vessel before replacing it.
rows.anchor: نعم مررت على عير بني فلان وهي بالروجاء وقد أضلوا بعيرا لهم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: He foretold that a camel would bolt from two riders near Banū Murra, throwing one and breaking his hand; they confirmed it as another sign.
rows.anchor: ومررت بعير فلان وفلان وفلان راكبان قعودا لهما ببني مرة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: He described Quraysh’s caravan, its loads and people, and a leading gray camel; observers saw it arrive at sunrise as foretold, yet disbelieved.
rows.anchor: يتقدمها بعير أورق فيها فلان وفلان كما قال لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names the initial journey to Jerusalem; the ascent followed the Isra. The Prophet disclosed Jerusalem first because leading with the heavenly ascent would have provoked disbelief.
rows.anchor: كان ابتدأ أمر المعراج كان المسري، والعروج كان بعد الإسراء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Jerusalem account became credible and established the proof, the Prophet told them of his ascent to the highest heaven and the Lote Tree.
rows.anchor: فلما تمكن ذلك في قلوبهم وبان لهم صدقة وقامت الحجة عليهم له،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account connects the ascent with the later description of drawing near, “two bow-lengths or nearer.”
rows.anchor: حتى دنا فتدلى فكان قاب قوسين أو أدنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave Moses the Book as guidance for the Children of Israel, just as He sent Muhammad on the night journey; they must take no other lord, partner, or guarantor.
rows.anchor: وجعلناه هدى لبني إسرائيل الآية يعني ألا تتخذوا من دوني وكيلا ربا وشريكا وكفيلا

rows.speaker: العامة
rows.claim: The common reading has third-person plural “they take,” understood as God telling the Israelites not to take a guardian besides Him.
rows.anchor: قرأه العامة: يتخذوا بالياء، يعني قلنا لهم لا يتخذوا.

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayd prefers the third-person reading, also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Abū ʿAmr, because it continues the report about Noah’s descendants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس ومجاهد وأبو عمر: بالياء واختاره أبو عبيد قال: لأنه خبر عنهم ذرية من حملنا مع نوح

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators say Noah was called grateful because he praised God whenever he dressed, ate, or drank.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: كان نوح (عليه السلام) إذا لبس ثوبا يأكل طعاما أو شرب شرابا.

rows.speaker: النظر بن شقي
rows.claim: A report from ʿImrān ibn Sulaym says Noah thanked God for food, drink, clothing, guidance, and relief from bodily harm, recognizing God could have withheld each.
rows.anchor: روى النظر بن شقي عن عمران بن سليم قال: إنما سمي نوح (عليه السلام) عبدا شكورا

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ḥudhayfa says Israel’s rebellion and killing of prophets brought Nebuchadnezzar against them; he entered Jerusalem, killed many, and carried off its people and temple treasure.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم «إن بني إسرائيل لما اعتدوا وعتوا وقتلوا الأنبياء بعث الله عليهم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Nebuchadnezzar ruled seven hundred years, killed seventy thousand over John son of Zechariah’s blood, and plundered Jerusalem’s treasure.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم «إن بني إسرائيل لما اعتدوا وعتوا وقتلوا الأنبياء بعث الله عليهم ملك فارس بخت نصر،

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: After a century of captivity, God moved the believing Persian king Cyrus to rescue the Israelites and return Jerusalem’s treasure; they then obeyed for a century.
rows.anchor: ثم إن الله تعالى رحمهم فأوحى إلى ملك من ملوك فارس يقال له كورس وكان مؤمنا

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: After Israel returned to sin, Antiochus attacked and burned Jerusalem; further sin brought a Roman ruler who captured them and burned the city again.
rows.anchor: ثم إنهم عادوا في المعاصي فسلط عليهم ملكا يقال له: إنطياخوش

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The report says the temple treasure will be returned to Jerusalem by the Mahdi, arriving by a fleet landed at Jaffa.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «فهذا من صفة حلي بيت المقدس ويرده المهدي إلى بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq frames Israel’s later history as a revealed account: God had tolerated their sins, and prophets guided rulers back to Torah and obedience.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار: كان مما أنزل الله على موسى في خبر عن بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
rows.claim: During King Ṣiddīqā’s reign, God sent Isaiah son of Amoz, who foretold a donkey-rider and, after him, a camel-rider.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار: كان مما أنزل الله على موسى في خبر عن بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
rows.claim: When wrongdoing increased after that king’s reign, Sennacherib of Babylon approached Jerusalem with six hundred thousand banners.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار: كان مما أنزل الله على موسى في خبر عن بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isaiah told King Ṣiddīqā that God ordered him to appoint a successor because he would die; the king prayed, and God extended his life by fifteen years and saved him from Sennacherib.
rows.anchor: أوحى الله تعالى إلى شعياء النبي (عليه السلام) أن ائت ملك بني إسرائيل فمره أن يوصي بوصيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king recovered after God prescribed applying figs to his ulcer; God then announced that Sennacherib’s army would die except for Sennacherib and five scribes.
rows.anchor: وقد أخر أجله خمس عشر سنة فأنجاه من عدوه سنحاريب ملك بابل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelite king found Sennacherib and five scribes alive after the rest of the army died and captured them.
rows.anchor: فأدركه الطلب في مفازة ومعه خمسة من كتابه أحدهم بخت نصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sennacherib admitted he ignored warnings and was overcome by folly; the Israelite king said he had been spared to bring greater punishment and warn Babylon.
rows.anchor: قد أتاني خبر ربكم ونصره إياكم ورحمته التي رحمكم بها قبل أن أخرج من بلادك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At God’s command Isaiah had the king release Sennacherib and his companions to warn their people; they returned to Babylon and described Israel’s divine protection.
rows.anchor: فأوحى الله إلى شعياء النبي (عليه السلام) : أن قل لملك بني إسرائيل ليرسل سنحاريب ومن معه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sennacherib died after seven years; his successor repeated his oppressive rule, while the Israelites ignored Isaiah until God commanded him to speak again.
rows.anchor: ثم لبث سنحاريب بعد ذلك سبع سنين ثم مات، واستخلف [بعده] ابن ابنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isaiah compares Israel to lost sheep whom God gathered, healed, and nourished; they grew arrogant and destroyed one another instead of recognizing their benefactor.
rows.anchor: وهم كالغنم الضائعة التي لا راعي لها، فآوى شاردتها وجمع ضالتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isaiah’s parable depicts God restoring a ruined land with a wall, palace, river, steward, and orchard; its plants yielded rotten fruit, representing Israel’s evil deeds.
rows.anchor: قال الله لهم: فإن الجدار ذمتي وإن القصر شريعتي وإن النهر كتابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall is God’s covenant, palace His law, river His Book, steward a prophet, plants the people, and rotten fruit their evil deeds.
rows.anchor: وإن القيم نبي وإن الغراس هم وإن الخروب الذي أطلع الغراس أعمالهم الخبيثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel claimed to approach God through animal sacrifice while shedding forbidden blood; they built mosques while corrupting their hearts and bodies.
rows.anchor: يتقربون إلي بذبح البقر والغنم وليس ينالني اللحم ولا أكله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God says sanctuaries are for remembrance, praise, and prayer as landmarks, not residences for God.
rows.anchor: إنما أمرت برفعها لأذكر فيها وأسبح ولتكون معلما لمن أراد أن يصلي فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel doubted God could unite their hearts, so He joined two dry sticks into one as proof of His power to reconcile and guide hearts.
rows.anchor: إني قد قدرت على أن أفقه العيدان اليابسة وعلى أن أؤالف بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel complained their fasting, prayer, charity, and supplication went unanswered; God says false speech and unlawful food undermine fasting and disloyal hearts undermine prayer.
rows.anchor: فكيف أرفع صيامهم وهم يلبسونه بقول الزور [ويتقوون] عليه بطعمة الحرام؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their charity earns reward for the people whose money they seized, and their prayers are merely words because their actions are distant from what they say.
rows.anchor: وهم يتصدقون بأموال غيرهم وإنما أؤجر عليها أهلها المغصوبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God responds to the humble and hears the oppressed; divine approval is shown by caring for poor and weak people and giving each claimant their due.
rows.anchor: وإن من علامة رضاي رضا المساكين، فلو رحموا المساكين وقربوا الضعفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The required justice includes defending the wronged and dispossessed and giving orphans, widows, the poor, and every rights-holder their due.
rows.anchor: ونصروا المغصوب والمغلوب وأعدلوا الغائب [وأدوا] إلى اليتيم والأرملة والمسكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God directly addressed humanity, He would illuminate their sight, hearing, and understanding and strengthen their bodily faculties.
rows.anchor: وإذا لكنت نور أبصارهم وسمع آذانهم ومعقول قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel dismissed revelation as fabricated or inherited tales and claimed they could compose its like or learn the unseen from demons.
rows.anchor: إنها أقاويل متقولة وأحاديث متوارثة وتأليف كما يؤلف السحرة والكهنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows what people reveal and conceal and has fixed an inevitable appointed time for His decree; claimants to unseen knowledge should state when it will occur.
rows.anchor: وأعلم ما يبدون وما كنتم يكتمون وإني قد قضيت يوم خلقت السماء والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage challenges them to produce the power behind God’s decree and says He will make His religion prevail despite the polytheists.
rows.anchor: فليأتوا بمثل القدرة التي بها أمضيت فإني مظهره على الدين كله ولو كره المشركون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine speech foretells a prophet named Aḥmad who will emerge after misguidance and ignorance, gentle, just, truthful, wise, and guided by Islam.
rows.anchor: وأحمد اسمه أهدي به بعد الضلالة وأعلم به بعد الجهالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised prophet will restore dignity, fame, wealth, and unity, gathering divided peoples and making his community the best brought forth for humanity.
rows.anchor: وأجمع به بعد الفرقة وأولف به قلوبا مختلفة وأهواء متشتتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His community will command right, forbid wrong, worship in every posture, fight in God’s cause, and leave homes and possessions seeking God’s approval.
rows.anchor: يأمرون بالمعروف وينهون عن المنكر إيمانا بي وتوحيدا لي وإخلاصا بي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community praises God in every setting, carries scripture in its hearts, is devout at night and valiant by day; this is God’s favor.
rows.anchor: قربانهم دماؤهم وأناجيلهم في صدورهم رهابين في الليل ليوث في النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel killed Isaiah after he fled into a tree; Satan exposed his garment, and they sawed through the tree and the prophet inside it.
rows.anchor: فلما فرغ نبيهم شعياء إليهم من مقالته عدوا عليه ليقتلوه فهرب منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Isaiah’s death God appointed Nāshiya son of Amūṣ and sent al-Khiḍr, identified as Irmiyā son of Ḥalfiyā from Aaron’s tribe.
rows.anchor: [فاستخلف الله] على بني إسرائيل بعد قتلهم شعياء رجلا منهم يقال له ناشية بن أموص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Khiḍr was so named because he sat on white fur that turned green when he rose; God says He chose and purified Irmiyā before birth.
rows.anchor: فأما سمي الخضر لأنه جلس على فروة بيضاء فقام [عنها وهي تهتز] خضراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nebuchadnezzar entered Jerusalem, killed Israelites, destroyed the Temple, filled it with soil, and took captives to Babylon.
rows.anchor: دخل بخت نصر وجنوده بيت المقدس فوطئ الشام وقتل بني إسرائيل حتى أفناهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nebuchadnezzar selected seventy thousand Israelite boys; allies received four boys each, including Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael.
rows.anchor: فاختار منهم بسبعين ألف صبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account identifies Nebuchadnezzar and his forces as the first punishment promised in the verse.
rows.anchor: فكانت هذه الواقعة الأولى التي أنزل الله ببني إسرائيل بأحداثهم وظلمهم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr tells of an Israelite who dreamed that an orphan in Babylon named Nebuchadnezzar would destroy Jerusalem, then sought him out.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير قال: كان رجل

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: The Israelite cared for sick Nebuchadnezzar with food, clothing, and money; Nebuchadnezzar asked for written protection if he ever became king.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير قال: كان رجل

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Nebuchadnezzar advised the Persian king that Syria was vulnerable; sent with four hundred thousand cavalry, he raided it and was chosen king on his return.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: وقال صاحب الطليعة لبخت نصر

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī gives another account: an Israelite dreamed that an orphan from Babylon would destroy Israel, then befriended Nebuchadnezzar and obtained a written promise of safety.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي بإسناده: إن رجلا من بني إسرائيل رأى في النوم أن خراب بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelite king wanted to marry his wife’s daughter, but John son of Zechariah forbade it; her mother arranged John’s beheading by manipulating the drunken king.
rows.anchor: فبلغ ذلك أمها فحقدت على [يحيى] حين نهاه أن يتزوج ابنتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The girl demanded John’s head on a platter; after his beheading, his head spoke against the unlawful act and his blood boiled despite being covered with earth.
rows.anchor: فلما أبت عليه بعث إليه فأتى برأسه [والرأس يتكلم] في الطشت حين وضع بين يديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A woman told Nebuchadnezzar’s army to divide into four groups and invoke God by John’s blood; the city fell, and he killed seventy thousand until the blood quieted.
rows.anchor: فنادوا: إنا نستفتحك يا الله بدم يحيى بن زكريا فإنها سوف تساقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woman said God required killing John’s killer and those who approved it; a written pardon protected the king’s family while Jerusalem was destroyed.
rows.anchor: فإن الله تعالى إذا قتل نبي لم يرض حتى يقتل من قتله ومن رضى قتله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Jerusalem fell, Nebuchadnezzar took prominent Israelites, including Daniel and other descendants of prophets, to Babylon.
rows.anchor: فلما خربه بخت نصر ذهبت معه بوجوه بني إسرائيل وأشرافهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Magi accused Daniel and his companions of worshiping another god; the king cast them into a pit with a fierce lion, but they were unharmed and a seventh figure appeared.
rows.anchor: فألقوا فيه وهم ستة وألقى معهم سبعا ضاريا ليأكلهم

rows.speaker: راهب
rows.claim: A monk’s report says Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a metal statue, a growing stone, and a tree; Daniel interpreted the visions.
rows.anchor: وهو ما روى إسماعيل بن عبد الكريم عن عبد الصمد بن معقل أنه سمع راهبا يقول: إن بخت نصر رأى في آخر زمانه

rows.speaker: دانيال
rows.claim: Daniel interprets the statue’s gold head as Nebuchadnezzar, silver as his son, bronze as the next kingdom, and iron as Persia.
rows.anchor: عبرها له دانيال (عليه السلام) . قال: أما الصنم الذي رأيت فأتيت الرأس الذهب فأنت أفضل الملوك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stone growing to fill the world represents a final prophet whose rule will displace the kingdoms and extend from east to west.
rows.anchor: وأما الحجر الذي ربا حتى ملأ ما بين المشرق والمغرب فنبي يبعثه الله في آخر الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daniel says clay legs represent divided, fragile Persian rule, while the tree’s destruction foretells Nebuchadnezzar losing his kingdom.
rows.anchor: وأما الرجل من فخار فتفرق أهل فارس فرقتين ولا يكون فيهم حينئذ قوام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nebuchadnezzar becomes ruler of birds, cattle, and wild beasts for seven years, retaining a human heart so he learns God rules all.
rows.anchor: في ذلك كله قلبك قلب إنسان حتى تعلم أن الله له ملك السماوات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God restores Nebuchadnezzar to human form and kingship, after which he believes and calls people to God.
rows.anchor: ثم رد الله إليه ملكه فأمن ودعا الناس إلى الله

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih says scriptural communities differed on whether Nebuchadnezzar died believing or whether his crimes made repentance unacceptable.
rows.anchor: [وسئل وهب بن منبه] أكان مؤمنا؟ قال: وجدت أهل الكتاب قد اختلفوا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further story says Nebuchadnezzar ordered the first man leaving to urinate killed; God prevented Daniel from going and the porter killed Nebuchadnezzar instead.
rows.anchor: فحبس الله عن دانيال البول وكان أول من قام من القوم يريد البول بخت نصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Ibn Isḥāq’s alternative account, Nebuchadnezzar demanded a way to ascend to heaven; a gnat entered his nose and killed him, demonstrating God’s power.
rows.anchor: فبعث الله عليه بقدرته بعوضة ليرى ضعفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God restored the surviving Israelites to Jerusalem and Syria, where they rebuilt and prospered; Ezra restored their burned Torah, as recounted earlier.
rows.anchor: وردهم إلى إيليا والشام فبنوا فيها وأربوا وكثروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects reports that Nebuchadnezzar invaded after John’s killing: historians and scriptural communities place the invasion at Isaiah’s killing in Irmiyā’s era.
rows.anchor: غلط [أهل السير] والأخبار والعلم بأمور الماضين من أهل الكتاب والمسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says 461 years elapsed from Nebuchadnezzar’s destruction of Jerusalem to John’s death, including seventy years to rebuilding and eighty-eight to Alexander.
rows.anchor: ذلك أنهم يعدون من لدن تخريب بخت نصر بيت المقدس إلى حين [عمارته في عهد كوسك] سبعين سنة

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq’s chronology is preferred: after return and rebuilding, Israel again sinned; God forgave them and sent prophets, some of whom they rejected or killed.
rows.anchor: وإنما الصحيح من ذلك ما ذكر محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
rows.claim: Authorities differ over the king’s intended bride: Ibn al-Zubayr says she was his daughter, al-Suddī his niece, and Ibn ʿAbbās his brother’s daughter.
rows.anchor: في قول عبد الله ابن الزبير وابنة أخته في قول السدي وابنة أخيه في قول ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers Ibn ʿAbbās’s identification of the woman as the king’s brother’s daughter, since John and Jesus forbade marrying a brother’s daughter.
rows.anchor: وهو الأصح إن شاء الله، لما روى الأعمش عن المنهال عن سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
rows.claim: After Zechariah’s death and John’s murder, a Babylonian king named Khardūs attacked Israel and ordered Nabor Zadan to kill them.
rows.anchor: رجعنا إلى حديث ابن إسحاق، فلما رفع الله موسى من بين أظهرهم وقتلوا يحيى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nabor Zadan found blood boiling at the altar; Israelites said it was John’s blood, shed after they rejected his warnings.
rows.anchor: [فوجد فيها دما يغلي] فسألهم عنه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel revealed that the boiling blood was John’s: they had killed him for warning them, and vengeance continued until Nabor Zadan invoked God and the blood stopped.
rows.anchor: إن هذا دم نبي منا كان ينهاها عن أمور كثيرة من سخط الله

rows.speaker: نبور زاذان
rows.claim: After the blood quieted, Nabor Zadan professed exclusive worship of God, rejecting any partner or child; God revealed he was faithful and truthful.
rows.anchor: فله الحكم والعلم والعزة والجبروت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another version says Nabor Zadan staged the required blood in a trench with slaughtered livestock and earlier corpses, satisfying Khardūs’s demand and ending the killing.
rows.anchor: فذبحها حتى سال الدم في العسكر وأمر بالقتلى الذين كانوا قتلوا قبل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account calls Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign the first punishment and Khardūs’s the final one; Israel later recovered under Greek and Roman rule, then Titus expelled them.
rows.anchor: وكانت الوقعة الأولى: بخت نصر وجنوده ثم رد الله لهم الكرة عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jerusalem remained ruined until ʿUmar ordered Muslims to rebuild it; later Israelite transgressions brought humiliation under other nations.
rows.anchor: وبقي بيت المقدس خرابا إلى أيام عمر بن الخطاب (رضي الله عنه) عمره المسلمين بأمره.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Abū Bishr reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr identifying Marḥā and Goliath among attackers; repeated sins later brought Roman rulers and Shapur.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو عوانة عن أبي بشير قال: سألت سعيد بن جبير عن قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda instead identifies Goliath’s attack and David’s kingship as the first defeat and restoration, and Nebuchadnezzar’s sack as the second punishment.
rows.anchor: قتادة في هذه الآية (وقضينا) قضى على القوم كما تسمعون فبعث عليهم في الأولى جالوت

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God showed mercy after Nebuchadnezzar, then punished Israel again and finally sent the Arabs, as foretold in 7:167.
rows.anchor: ثم بعث الله عليهم هذا الحي من العرب كما قال: وإذ تأذن ربك ليبعثن عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We decreed to Israel in the Book” means God informed them through revealed books; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda instead read it as decreeing against them, with the Book as the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: وقضينا إلى بني إسرائيل في الكتاب أي أخبرناهم وعلمناهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the first corruption was violating Torah rulings, disobeying God and Moses, committing forbidden acts, and transgressing against people.
rows.anchor: فعلى قول قتادة: إفسادهم في المرة الأولى ما خالفوا من أحكام التوراة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī, reporting from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd, identifies the first corruption as killing Zechariah.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: في خبر ذكره عن أبي مالك وأبي جهل عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq identifies the first corruption as Israel’s killing of Isaiah son of Amoz under Irmiyā.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: إن إفسادهم في المرة الأولى قتلهم شعياء بن أمصيا

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Isḥāq says Zechariah died naturally and Isaiah was the prophet killed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: إن بعض أهل العلم أخبره أن زكريا مات موتا ولم يقتل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda and al-ʿAwfī’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās identify the attackers as Goliath al-Jazarī and his troops, whom David defeated.
rows.anchor: بعثنا عليكم عبادا لنا يعني [جالوت الجزري] وجنوده وهو الذي قتله داود

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Abū al-Maʿlā and Yaʿlā report from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that the attackers were Sennacherib’s people from Nineveh.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو المعلى ويعلى عن سعيد بن جبير: هم صحاريب من أهل نينوى

rows.speaker: أبو بشير
rows.claim: Abū Bishr’s report from Saʿīd gives Ṣarkhān al-Khazrī as the attacker; Ibn Isḥāq instead names Babylonian Nebuchadnezzar and his men.
rows.anchor: أبو بشير عنه: صرخان الخزري، وقال: ابن إسحاق: بخت نصر البابلي وأصحابه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ulū baʾs” means forceful in war; Ibn ʿAbbās says “jāsū” means they walked through the houses.
rows.anchor: أولي بأس يعني بطش، وفي الحرب شديد فجاسوا أي خافوا وداروا.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ glosses “jāsū” as killing Israelites among their homes.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: مشوا، الفراء: قتلوكم بين بيوتكم.

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says “jāsū” means searching through the houses.
rows.anchor: أبو عبيدة: طلبوا ما فيها كما يجوس الرجل الأخبار أي يطلبها .

rows.speaker: القتيبي
rows.claim: Al-Qutaybī explains that the attackers lived among, killed, and corrupted the people.
rows.anchor: القتيبي: [عاشوا وقتلوا] وأفسدوا .

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr reconciles the glosses: the attackers roamed through homes seeking and killing Israelites as they went back and forth.
rows.anchor: ابن جرير: طافوا من الديار يطلبونهم ويقتلونهم ذاهبين وجائين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās read “faḥāsū” with ḥāʾ instead of jīm, with the same meaning.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس: فحاسوا بالحاء ومعناها واحد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A promise fulfilled” is an inescapable decree; “the turn” means return and renewed power, accompanied by wealth, children, and greater numbers.
rows.anchor: وكان وعدا مفعولا قضاء كائنا لا خلف فيه ثم رددنا لكم الكرة الرجعة والدولة عليهم وأمددناكم بأموال وبنين وجعلناكم أكثر نفيرا عددا

rows.speaker: القتيبي
rows.claim: Al-Qutaybī defines “nafir” as a man’s accompanying relatives and household, and connects the noun to “nāfir.”
rows.anchor: قال القتيبي: والنفير من نفر مع الرجل من عشيرته وأهل بيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doing good benefits and rewards the doer; “for it” can mean “upon it,” as in “peace be upon you.”
rows.anchor: إن أحسنتم يا بني إسرائيل أحسنتم لأنفسكم لها ثوابا ونفعها وإن أسأتم فلها أي فعليها كقوله فسلام لك أي عليك.

rows.speaker: محمد بن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr reads “for it” with the sense “to it,” as in the verse saying God inspired the earth; another gloss makes it recompense or punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن جرير: قالها كما قال بأن ربك أوحى لها أي إليها

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl glosses “for it” as meaning that the soul has a Lord who forgives wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسين بن الفضل: يعني فلها رب يغفر الإساءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later promise is linked to Israel’s attempts to kill Jesus, who was raised, and their killing of John; Persians and Romans then killed, captured, expelled, and dispossessed them.
rows.anchor: فإذا جاء وعد الآخرة أي المرة الآخرة من إفسادكم وذلك على قصدهم قتل عيسى (عليه السلام) يحيى حين رفع

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī reads the verb with first-person plural nūn and fatḥa, matching the surrounding verbs; the reading is also reported from ʿAlī.
rows.anchor: فقرأ الكسائي: لنسوؤ بالنون وفتح الهمزة على التعظيم اعتبارا

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s reading “we shall surely make your faces suffer” adds nūn and emphatic nūn.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبي بن كعب: لنسؤن وجوهكم بالنون وحرف التأكيد.

rows.speaker: أهل الكوفة
rows.claim: The Kufans read the verb in the third-person singular: either God or the enemy will make their faces suffer.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل الكوفة: بالياء على التوحيد

rows.speaker: باقي القراء
rows.claim: The remaining readers use a plural subject: the forceful servants will make their faces suffer, enter Jerusalem, and destroy what they conquered.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون: ليسوؤا وجوهكم بالياء وضم الهمزة على الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Tabbīr” means destruction of what the attackers conquered; “the mosque” is Jerusalem and its surroundings.
rows.anchor: وليَدْخُلُوا المسجد يعني بيت المقدس ونواحيه كما دخلوه أول مرة وليتبروا وليهلكوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains “if you return, We return” as renewed punishment for renewed sin; he says Muhammad was sent against them and they paid jizya subdued.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: وإن عدتم إلى المعصية عدنا إلى العقوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ḥaṣīr” means prison or confinement, from the root for restraint; Arabs also use it of a king secluded from people.
rows.anchor: وجعلنا جهنم للكافرين حصيرا معينا سجنا ومحبسا من الحصر وهو الحبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Labīd’s verse uses “al-ḥaṣīr” for the king’s gate; the root also describes speech that becomes stuck and a man abstaining from women.
rows.anchor: وقماقم غلب الرقاب كأنهم … جن لدى باب الحصير قيام

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets “ḥaṣīr” as a bed or resting place, citing the Arabs’ use of the word for a small mat; the author accepts this as sound.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وجعلنا جهنم للكافرين حصيرا أي فراشا ومهادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an guides to the soundest, fairest, and most upright way.
rows.anchor: إن هذا القرآن يهدي للتي هي أقوم أي الطريقة التي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It gives believers who do righteous deeds glad tidings of a great reward, namely Paradise.
rows.anchor: ويبشر المؤمنين الذين يعملون الصالحات أن لهم أجرا كبيرا وهو الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who do not believe in the Hereafter have a painful punishment prepared for them, namely Hell.
rows.anchor: الآخرة أعتدنا لهم عذابا أليما وهي النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final wāw of “yadʿu” is omitted in speech and writing but implied grammatically, for ease before a still lām; the author cites several parallel deletions.
rows.anchor: ويدع الإنسان حذفت الواو هنا في اللفظ والخط ولم يحذف في المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In anger people invoke harm against their wealth, children, and selves just as they ask for blessings; God mercifully does not hasten to answer harmful wishes.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الآية ويدع الإنسان على [ماله وولده ونفسه بالسوء]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such rash curses include “God curse him” or “destroy it”; they are the harmful counterpart of asking for health and safety.
rows.anchor: والغضب: اللهم العنه اللهم أهلكه دعاءه بالخير أي كدعائه ربه أن يهب له العافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s restraint parallels the verse saying that if He hastened evil as people hasten good, their term would be ended; humans are hasty in asking for what they dislike.
rows.anchor: نظيره قوله تعالى ولو يعجل الله للناس الشر استعجالهم بالخير لقضي إليهم أجلهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and other commentators say the human is hasty; Ibn ʿAbbās says he is impatient and lacks endurance in ease or hardship.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد وجماعة من المفسرين، وقال ابن عباس: [يريد] ضجرا لا صبرا له

rows.speaker: قوم من المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators identify the human in the verse specifically as Adam.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم من المفسرين: أراد الإنسان آدم.

rows.speaker: سلمان الفارسي
rows.claim: Salman al-Fārisī says Adam’s head was created first; seeing his body take shape, he asked God to hurry before night while his legs were not yet animated.
rows.anchor: قال سلمان الفارسي: أول ما خلق الله من آدم رأسه، فجعل ينظر وهو يخلق جسده

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that Adam admired his formed body and tried to rise before he could, illustrating haste.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس قال: لما خلق الله رأس آدم نظر إلى جسده فأعجبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says a captive escaped after Sawda released him; the Prophet regretted praying against her and asked that any such prayer become mercy, after which this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: فدعا النبي عليها بقطع اليد ثم ندم فقال: اللهم إنما أنا بشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day are signs of God’s oneness, existence, knowledge, and power; dimmed night and illuminating daylight let people work and count years.
rows.anchor: وجعلنا الليل والنهار آيتين دلالتين وعلامتين على وحدانيتنا ووجودنا

rows.speaker: أبو الطفيل
rows.claim: Abū al-Ṭufayl says Ibn al-Kawwāʾ asked ʿAlī about the dark mark in the moon, and ʿAlī identified it as the erasure of the night’s sign.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الطفيل: سأل ابن الكواء عليا (رضي الله عنه) فقال: ما هذا السواد في القمر؟

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the sun and moon each had seventy portions of light; sixty-nine were removed from the moon and added to the sun.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الله نور الشمس سبعين جزءا ونور القمر سبعين جزءا فمحا من نور القمر تسعة وستين جزءا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daylight’s sign is the sun, made bright and illuminating.
rows.anchor: وجعلنا آية النهار وهي الشمس مبصرة [منيرة مضيئة]

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلا
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ interprets daylight’s being “mubṣira” as its own illumination.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو بن العلا: يعني بصرها.

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī explains “mubṣira” through the Arabic expression “the day became perceptible,” meaning it grew bright.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي: هو من قول العرب أبصر النهار إذا أضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says the signs let people seek God’s bounty and count years; God has explained everything distinctly.
rows.anchor: لتبتغوا فضلا من ربكم إلى قوله فصلناه تفصيلا بيناه تبيينا.

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās says the sun and moon began as suns; God made one a moon and reduced its light so people could order work, worship, debts, farming, and rest.
rows.anchor: مقاتل بن علي عن عكرمة عن ابن عباس قال: سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول:

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the same report, Gabriel swept his wing across the moon’s face at God’s command, leaving its light and dark traces.
rows.anchor: مقاتل بن علي عن عكرمة عن ابن عباس قال: سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول:
